title: Fetching and Caching Data
summary: A React page can ask for data and show it when the answer arrives.
introduction: A React page can ask for data and show it when the answer arrives. Show a loading message while you wait and a helpful message if the request fails. Learn why an old answer should not replace a newer one.
learningObjectives: Cancel stale requests with AbortController in an effect
Fetch data with useQuery and render loading, error and success states
Update server data with useMutation and invalidate cached queries
Read a promise with use inside a Suspense boundary and know its limits

blocks.text: What the manual approach is missing

items: **No cache.** Navigating away and back fetches again, even if the data is seconds old.
**Duplicate requests.** Two components that need the same data send two requests.
**Boilerplate.** Every fetch repeats the status, error and ignore-flag code.
**No retries, no background refresh, no pagination helpers.**

blocks.text: None of this is a problem for a page with one request. It becomes one as soon as the same data appears in several places.

The `ignore` flag from the [effects lesson](/tutorials/react/effects) discards stale responses but still lets the request complete. `AbortController` cancels it, which saves bandwidth and matters for search boxes that fire a request per keystroke.

blocks.text: Aborting rejects the fetch promise with an `AbortError`, so the catch must ignore that name; everything else is a real error. The `signal` option is also accepted by most other HTTP clients.
TanStack Query (formerly React Query) keeps a cache of server data keyed by **query keys** and gives components hooks to read it. Install it and create one client at the root:

blocks.text: `queryKey` identifies the data in the cache; `queryFn` knows how to fetch it. Any component that calls `useQuery` with the key `['users']` shares the cached result, and only one request is sent even if several components mount at once. `staleTime` says how long a result counts as fresh; after that, mounting a component or refocusing the window triggers a background refetch while the old data stays on screen. `isPending` is true only while there is no data at all; `isFetching` is true during any request, including background ones.

Keys are arrays so that they can include variables. A query for one user should use `['users', id]`: changing `id` changes the key, which fetches and caches the new user separately and keeps the old one for an instant back navigation.

blocks.text: `useMutation` wraps a write. `invalidateQueries` marks every query whose key starts with `['todos']` as stale, which refetches the ones currently on screen, so the list updates without you touching its state.

React 19's `use` can read a promise: while it is pending React suspends the component and shows the nearest `<Suspense>` fallback; when it resolves the component renders with the value. The promise must be **stable**, created outside render or cached by a library, because a new promise on every render would suspend forever.

blocks.text: In a plain Vite app this pattern is mostly used through libraries: TanStack Query offers `useSuspenseQuery`, and React Router's data mode passes promises from loaders. Frameworks with Server Components go further and pass promises from the server. Knowing the primitive helps you read those APIs; writing the promise cache yourself is rarely worth it.

blocks.title: Common mistake: creating the promise inside the component
blocks.text: `const data = use(fetch('/api/quote'))` starts a new request on every render. Each render creates a new promise, `use` suspends on it, the fallback shows, React retries the render, and a new promise appears again. Create the promise once, outside the component or in a cache, and pass it in.

questions.question: What does `queryKey: ['users', id]` achieve compared with `queryKey: ['users']`?
questions.explanation: The key is the cache address. Including `id` gives every user a separate entry, so switching ids fetches the new user and keeps the previous one cached.
options: Nothing; extra key elements are ignored
Each id gets its own cache entry, so changing id fetches and caches that user separately
It disables caching for that query
It makes the query run only once

questions.question: `invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] })` deletes the cached todos immediately, so the list goes blank until the refetch finishes.
questions.explanation: Invalidation marks the data stale and refetches active queries in the background. The old data stays on screen until the new response replaces it.
